$$
\begin{aligned}p+6-12 & =-(p-2) \\ p-6 & =-p+2 \\ 2p & =8 \\ p & =4\end{aligned}

$$
\text{LCM}(3z,6z)=6z.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2z-1}{6z}=\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z} \\ 6z\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{6z}) & =6z\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{3z}+\frac{z-1}{6z}) \\ 6z\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{6z}) & =6z\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{3z})+6z\cdot (\frac{z-1}{6z}) \\ \cancel{6z}\cdot (\frac{2z-1}{\cancel{6z}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{3z}\cdot (\frac{3z-1}{\cancel{3z}})+\cancel{6z}\cdot (\frac{z-1}{\cancel{6z}}) \\ 2z-1 & =2\cdot (3z-1)+z-1\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Which value of $x$ satisfies the equation $\frac{1}{x}=\frac{2+x}{2x}+\frac{3}{4x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $x,2x,$ and $4x.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(x,2x,4x)=4x.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $4x,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} & =\frac{2+x}{2x}+\frac{3}{4x} \\ 4x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) & =4x\cdot (\frac{2+x}{2x}+\frac{3}{4x}) \\ 4x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) & =4x\cdot (\frac{2+x}{2x})+4x\cdot (\frac{3}{4x}) \\ 4x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) & =2\cdot 2x\cdot (\frac{2+x}{2x})+4x\cdot (\frac{3}{4x}) \\ 4\cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{x}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{2x}\cdot (\frac{2+x}{\cancel{2x}})+\cancel{4x}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{4x}}) \\ 4\cdot (1) & =2\cdot (2+x)+3 \\ 4 & =2(2+x)+3\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =2(2+x)+3 \\ 4 & =4+2x+3 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=-\frac{3}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=-\frac{3}{2}.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x})-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}}) \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{3x-1}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) & =x\cdot \cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{2}{\cancel{x}})-\cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{x-3}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) \\ (3x-1) & =x\cdot 2-(x-3) \\ (3x-1) & =2x-(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-1) & =2x-(x-3) \\ 3x-1 & =2x-x+3 \\ 3x-1 & =x+3 \\ 3x-x & =3+1 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=2.$

questions.problem: Which value of $m$ satisfies the equation $\frac{3}{m}-\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}}=\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2{m}^{2},$ ${m}^{2}$ and $m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(m,{m}^{2},2{m}^{2})=2{m}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2{m}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{m}-\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{{m}^{2}} \\ 2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{m}-\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}}) & =2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}) \\ 2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{m})-2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3m+4}{2{m}^{2}}) & =2{m}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{{m}^{2}}) \\ 2m\cdot \cancel{m}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{m}})-\cancel{2{m}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{3m+4}{\cancel{2{m}^{2}}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{{m}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{{m}^{2}}}) \\ 2m\cdot 3-(3m+4) & =2\cdot 1 \\ 6m-(3m+4) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6m-(3m+4) & =2 \\ 6m-3m-4 & =2 \\ 3m & =6 \\ m & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=2.$

We note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $n$ and ${n}^{2}.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(n,{n}^{2})={n}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${n}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{6}{n} \\ {n}^{2}(\frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}}) & ={n}^{2}(\frac{6}{n}) \\ {n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+{n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}} & ={n}^{2}\cdot \frac{6}{n} \\ {n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+{n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}} & =n\cdot n\cdot \frac{6}{n} \\ \cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot \frac{n+7}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}}+\cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot \frac{n-5}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}} & =n\cdot \cancel{n}\cdot \frac{6}{\cancel{n}} \\ n+7+n-5 & =n\cdot 6\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $n,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}n+7+n-5 & =n\cdot 6 \\ 2n+2 & =6n \\ -4n & =-2 \\ n & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $n=0$ as a solution. But since $n=\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $n=\frac{1}{2}.$

We note that $b=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $36b$ and $12{b}^{2}.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(36b,12{b}^{2})=36{b}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $36{b}^{2},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}} & =-\frac{12}{36b}+\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}} \\ 36{b}^{2}\cdot (\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) & =36{b}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{12}{36b}+\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) \\ 36{b}^{2}\cdot (\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) & =36{b}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{12}{36b})+36{b}^{2}\cdot (\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) \\ 3\cdot 12{b}^{2}\cdot (\frac{5b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) & =b\cdot 36b\cdot (-\frac{12}{36b})+3\cdot 12{b}^{2}\cdot (\frac{4b+8}{12{b}^{2}}) \\ 3\cdot \cancel{12{b}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{5b+8}{\cancel{12{b}^{2}}}) & =b\cdot \cancel{36b}\cdot (-\frac{12}{\cancel{36b}})+3\cdot \cancel{12{b}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{4b+8}{\cancel{12{b}^{2}}}) \\ 3(5b+8) & =-12b+3(4b+8)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $b,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(5b+8) & =-12b+3(4b+8) \\ 15b+24 & =-12b+12b+24 \\ 15b+24 & =24 \\ 15b & =24-24 \\ 15b & =0 \\ b & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $b=0$ as a solution. Since $b=0,$ we conclude that there is no solution.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations Containing One Distinct Linear Denominator
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x = 0$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. Both denominators in the equation are $x,$ so the least common denominator is $x.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $x$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{x} & =\frac{x-4}{x}+2 \\ x\cdot (\frac{x+2}{x}) & =x\cdot (\frac{x-4}{x}+2) \\ x\cdot \frac{x+2}{x} & =x\cdot \frac{x-4}{x}+x\cdot 2 \\ \cancel{x}\cdot \frac{x+2}{\cancel{x}} & =\cancel{x}\cdot \frac{x-4}{\cancel{x}}+2x \\ x+2 & =x-4+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =x-4+2x \\ x+2 & =3x-4 \\ 3x-x & =2+4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=3$ is different from $x=0,$ we accept it as a solution. 

Therefore, the solution is $x=3.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations Containing Two Distinct Linear Denominators
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $8x$ and $2x,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is

$$
\textrm{LCM}(8x,2x) = 8x.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $8x$ and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3-\frac{10x+7}{8x} & =\frac{6x-3}{2x} \\ 8x\cdot (3-\frac{10x+7}{8x}) & =8x\cdot (\frac{6x-3}{2x}) \\ 8x\cdot 3-8x\cdot (\frac{10x+7}{8x}) & =8x\cdot (\frac{6x-3}{2x}) \\ 24x-\cancel{8x}\cdot (\frac{10x+7}{\cancel{8x}}) & =4\cdot \cancel{2x}\cdot (\frac{6x-3}{\cancel{2x}}) \\ 24x-(10x+7) & =4\cdot (6x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}24x-(10x+7) & =4\cdot (6x-3) \\ 14x-7 & =24x-12 \\ 24x-14x & =-7+12 \\ 10x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x= \dfrac 12$ is different from $x=0,$ we accept it as a solution. 

Therefore, the solution is $x= \dfrac 12.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Rational Equations Containing Three Distinct Linear Denominators
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that $x = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $x, 6x,$ and $3x,$ so the the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is

$$
\textrm{LCM}(x, 6x, 3x) = 6x.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $6x$ and simplifying, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+x}{x}+\frac{5+x}{6x} & =\frac{1-x}{3x} \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x}+\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =6x\cdot \frac{1-x}{3x} \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x})+6x\cdot (\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =6x\cdot (\frac{1-x}{3x}) \\ 6x\cdot (\frac{1+x}{x})+6x\cdot (\frac{5+x}{6x}) & =2\cdot 3x\cdot (\frac{1-x}{3x}) \\ 6\cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{1+x}{\cancel{x}})+\cancel{6x}\cdot (\frac{5+x}{\cancel{6x}}) & =2\cdot \cancel{3x}\cdot (\frac{1-x}{\cancel{3x}}) \\ 6(1+x)+(5+x) & =2(1-x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(1+x)+(5+x) & =2(1-x) \\ 6+6x+5+x & =2-2x \\ 7x+11 & =2-2x \\ 7x+2x & =2-11 \\ 9x & =-9 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. Since $x=-1$ is different from $x=0,$ we can accept it as the solution.

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that $a = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

Now, let's multiply both sides of the equation by the least common denominator. The equation has the denominators $3a^2,$ $a,$ and $2a^2,$ so the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators is

$$
\textrm{LCM}(3a^2, a, 2a^2) = 6a^2.
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $6a^2$ and simplifying, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}+\frac{1}{a} & =\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}} \\ 6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}}+\frac{1}{a}) & =6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}) \\ 6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}})+6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{a}) & =6{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot 3{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{3{a}^{2}})+6a\cdot a\cdot (\frac{1}{a}) & =3\cdot 2{a}^{2}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{2{a}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot \cancel{3{a}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{2a-5}{\cancel{3{a}^{2}}})+6a\cdot \cancel{a}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{a}}) & =3\cdot \cancel{2{a}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{a-1}{\cancel{2{a}^{2}}}) \\ 2\cdot (2a-5)+6a\cdot (1) & =3\cdot (a-1) \\ 2(2a-5)+6a & =3(a-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $a,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(2a-5)+6a & =3(a-1) \\ 4a-10+6a & =3a-3 \\ 10a-10 & =3a-3 \\ 10a-3a & =-3+10 \\ 7a & =7 \\ a & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall that we cannot allow $a=0$ as a solution. Since $a=1$ is different from $a=0,$ we can accept it as a solution.

Therefore, the solution is $a=1.$
